controls.label: Query matrix Q
controls.help: Sets the query rows; changing Q changes the scores matrix and therefore the weights, row sums and output.

controls.label: Key matrix K
controls.help: Sets the key rows; changing K changes the scores matrix and therefore the weights, row sums and output.

controls.label: Value matrix V
controls.help: Sets the value rows that are averaged; changing V changes only the output matrix, not the scores or weights.

controls.label: Apply 1/sqrt(dk) scaling
controls.help: When on, scores are divided by sqrt(dk) before softmax, which changes the scores matrix and therefore the weights, row sums and output; when off, raw dot products are used.

explorations.title: Equal scores give uniform weights
explorations.instruction: Predict: when every dot product in a row is equal, what will the two attention weights be? Then apply the preset, which sets q_mat, k_mat and v_mat and turns use_scaling on.
explorations.observe: The weights heatmap shows 0.5 in both columns of both rows, the row sums readout shows 1.00 for each query, and the output heatmap shows 0.5 in every entry.
explorations.why: Both key rows are identical, so each dot product equals the first coordinate of the query; after dividing by sqrt(dk) the two scores in a row are equal, and softmax over equal scores returns 0.5 each. The output is then the average of the two value rows.

explorations.title: Scaling off makes a dominant score sharper
explorations.instruction: Predict: if we turn off the 1/sqrt(dk) scaling, will the larger score dominate the weights more or less? Then apply the preset, which sets q_mat, k_mat and v_mat and turns use_scaling off.
explorations.observe: For the first query the weights readout becomes about 0.9526 and 0.0474, while for the second query it becomes about 0.7311 and 0.2689; the row sums still read 1.00, and the output follows the first value row much more strongly in the first row.
explorations.why: Without scaling the scores matrix keeps the raw dot products 3 and 0 for the first query and 1 and 0 for the second; a larger positive score produces a larger exponential in softmax, so the first weight grows and the second shrinks. The scaling divisor would have reduced both scores before softmax.
